On Sat, Oct 25, 2008 at 4:19 AM, nongnone <anunc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear All,
> I am working on CNV mapping with SNP6.0. I have no idea to analyze
> them because I have only two samples (male and female). I would like
> to ask you for more information. Are two chips analyzed in your
> algorithm effect the CNV results ? I mean that the small sample size
> of chip effect the normalization or whatever step in your algorithm ?

My first question is what is your biological question/hypothesis
making you analyze only two single samples? That is a key question
for your analysis. What you expect to learn from CN estimates of two
samples alone? Are you doing personalized diagnostics?

I'm not sure which "algorithm" you refer to, but I guess you are
referring to the CRMA method. If so, please read:

H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]

carefully. There are also references to the other related methods
used in that study and those will give you more insights in CN
analysis.

Any microarray-based CN analysis requires some kind of reference to
which the sample of interest is compared to. This is pretty much the
case for all microarray analysis, not just CN ones. Your problem is
to choose/find a reference.

If you use the "default" CRMA processing steps, you are probably using
the pool of all arrays as a proxy for your reference. In your case
this means that you take the average of only two arrays, which is not
a good idea. This is basically the same as doing a pairwise CN
analysis of the two samples, which I guess you don't want.

As I've suggested others on this list (search archive) a few times: If
you have too few arrays in your data set, then try to get more
anonymous/dummy arrays from the *same* microarray facility, because
they will add to your pool to calculate the average reference, and
in-house data is always less noisy than external data. Some people
suggest to use publicly available HapMap CEL files (you have to order
them; free), but I and others have found that this adds much more
variability to the estimates.

Cheers

/Henrik
